questions.prompt: An administrator is away from their workstation and needs to inspect Azure resources from a browser. Which approach avoids installing Azure tools on the borrowed computer?

options.text: Deploy a dedicated administration VM first.
options.explanation: A VM supplies a custom environment, but Cloud Shell already provides the required browser administration without that deployment.

options.text: Open Azure Cloud Shell.
options.explanation: Cloud Shell supplies an authenticated browser shell with Azure tools already installed.

options.text: Install Azure CLI on the borrowed computer.
options.explanation: A local CLI can manage resources, but installation does not meet the requirement to avoid installing tools.

options.text: Create a new Azure subscription first.
options.explanation: A new subscription is not needed to open Cloud Shell and inspect resources the account can already access.

questions.prompt: An account has permission to view a VM but not delete it. What happens to that account’s Azure resource permissions when Cloud Shell opens?

options.text: The account can delete the VM because the tools are Microsoft-managed.
options.explanation: Microsoft managing the tools does not bypass the account’s resource authorization.

options.text: The account loses all existing permissions until a new role is assigned.
options.explanation: Cloud Shell uses existing permissions; opening it does not remove the account’s granted access.

options.text: The account keeps its existing resource permissions.
options.explanation: Cloud Shell authenticates the signed-in account; it does not elevate its Azure resource permissions.

options.text: The account gains Owner access to its subscription.
options.explanation: Opening a shell does not create an Owner role assignment or grant subscription-wide control.

questions.prompt: You want a diagnostic script to remain available after Cloud Shell closes and to use it next week from another device. Where should you save it?

options.text: In a temporary folder outside persistent storage.
options.explanation: Files outside persistent storage can disappear when the temporary session ends.

options.text: Only in the terminal’s command history on screen.
options.explanation: Displaying commands in the current terminal is not a way to persist the script file on the mounted share.

options.text: In an ephemeral session without attaching storage.
options.explanation: An ephemeral session does not provide storage that preserves these files for a later session.

options.text: In the clouddrive folder of the mounted Azure Files share.
options.explanation: The mounted share persists clouddrive files across temporary sessions and devices.

questions.prompt: A non-interactive maintenance script must keep running for an hour without user activity. Why is a temporary Cloud Shell session unsuitable?

options.text: It can time out after 20 minutes without interactive activity.
options.explanation: Cloud Shell is intended for interactive use; inactivity can terminate the session and its running work.

options.text: Cloud Shell only supports PowerShell, not Bash.
options.explanation: Cloud Shell supports both Bash and PowerShell; shell choice is not this workload’s problem.

options.text: Cloud Shell cannot authenticate an Azure account.
options.explanation: Cloud Shell automatically authenticates the signed-in account, so lack of authentication is not the limitation.

options.text: Every Cloud Shell command is limited to one minute.
options.explanation: The documented concern is the inactivity timeout, not a universal one-minute command limit.

questions.prompt: A required administration tool needs sudo during installation. Which environment choice meets that requirement?

options.text: Mount an Azure Files share to grant administrator privileges.
options.explanation: Storage mounting enables file persistence, not host privilege elevation.

options.text: Use a VM or container where you control the required privileges.
options.explanation: A custom environment can provide administrator privileges that the unprivileged Cloud Shell account lacks.

options.text: Run sudo in the existing Cloud Shell session.
options.explanation: Cloud Shell does not allow sudo or commands requiring elevated host permissions.

options.text: Switch Cloud Shell from Bash to PowerShell to gain root.
options.explanation: Changing shell does not elevate the user’s host permissions.

questions.prompt: You need to edit deploy.ps1 directly in Cloud Shell. Which command opens that file in the built-in editor?

options.text: Connect-AzAccount deploy.ps1
options.explanation: Connect-AzAccount handles Azure sign-in, not opening a file in the Cloud Shell editor.

options.text: kubectl deploy.ps1
options.explanation: kubectl manages Kubernetes resources; it is not the Cloud Shell file-editor command.

options.text: code deploy.ps1
options.explanation: The current Cloud Shell editor supports code <filename> to open a file for editing.

options.text: az login deploy.ps1
options.explanation: az login signs in to Azure; it does not open a script in the editor.

questions.prompt: One ARM template must deploy a storage account with different names in development and production. Which template feature should supply the name?

options.text: A fixed name hardcoded in resources.
options.explanation: A hardcoded name cannot vary by deployment without editing the template.

options.text: The contentVersion value.
options.explanation: contentVersion tracks the template’s version; it is not a replacement for a resource-name parameter.

options.text: A parameter referenced in the resource name.
options.explanation: Parameters accept environment-specific input, allowing the same resource definition to use different names.

options.text: An output containing the account name.
options.explanation: Outputs return deployment results; they do not supply the input used to name the resource.

questions.prompt: An ARM template needs a password supplied at deployment time. Which parameter design follows the module’s guidance?

options.text: Use an ordinary string with the production password as its default.
options.explanation: An ordinary string and hardcoded secret default do not follow the module’s secure-parameter guidance.

options.text: Put the password in a variable committed with the template.
options.explanation: A variable containing the password still hardcodes the secret in template source.

options.text: Return the password as an ordinary output instead of accepting a parameter.
options.explanation: An output is a deployment result, not a secure way to supply the password the resource needs.

options.text: Use secureString without a hardcoded password or secret default.
options.explanation: secureString is the suitable type for a password, and avoiding embedded secrets keeps them out of template source.

questions.prompt: A deployment should return a newly deployed storage account’s runtime endpoints. Which design fits the exercise?

options.text: Declare an output whose value uses reference(...).primaryEndpoints.
options.explanation: The reference function retrieves runtime resource properties, and outputs return the endpoint object after deployment.

options.text: Use allowedValues to discover the runtime endpoints.
options.explanation: allowedValues constrains parameter inputs; it does not query the deployed storage account.

options.text: Store the endpoint in contentVersion before deploying.
options.explanation: contentVersion identifies the template version and cannot discover the resource’s runtime endpoint.

options.text: Declare a secureString parameter and expect Azure to populate it automatically.
options.explanation: Parameters are deployment inputs; Azure does not use them as automatic return values for runtime endpoints.

questions.prompt: You deploy an unchanged template twice to the same resource group using the same resource names. What is the expected effect of template idempotence?

options.text: The template becomes read-only after its first deployment.
options.explanation: Idempotence describes repeatable resource deployment, not locking the template file after first use.

options.text: Existing unchanged resources are reused rather than duplicated.
options.explanation: With the same identities and unchanged settings, repeating the deployment does not create duplicate resources.

options.text: A second copy of every resource is created automatically.
options.explanation: Repeating the deployment with the same resource names does not automatically invent new resource identities.

options.text: The second deployment must fail because the names already exist.
options.explanation: ARM templates can redeploy and update existing resources; name reuse at the same scope is expected.

questions.prompt: The storageSKU parameter has allowedValues ["Standard_LRS", "Standard_ZRS"]. A deployment supplies "Basic". What should you expect?

options.text: Azure automatically adds Basic to the allowedValues list.
options.explanation: Deployment does not rewrite the template’s allowed input values.

options.text: The deployment creates all three listed or supplied SKUs.
options.explanation: The parameter selects one allowed value; it does not instruct ARM to create multiple accounts.

options.text: Parameter validation rejects the supplied value.
options.explanation: Basic is outside the allowedValues list, so the supplied input fails the parameter constraint.

options.text: Azure silently substitutes Standard_LRS.
options.explanation: A default applies when an input is omitted; it does not silently replace an explicitly invalid value.

questions.prompt: You redeploy an existing resource in incremental mode and omit a property previously set to a non-default value. Which assumption should you avoid?

options.text: Assuming the same resource identity can be updated.
options.explanation: Incremental deployments can update an existing resource using the same name and scope.

options.text: Assuming the template describes the desired resource state.
options.explanation: The resource definition should describe its final desired state, including required non-default properties.

options.text: Assuming unrelated resources omitted from an incremental template are left in place.
options.explanation: Incremental mode leaves resources absent from the template unchanged; that differs from properties omitted within a declared resource.

options.text: Assuming the omitted property necessarily keeps its previous value.
options.explanation: Incremental deployment reapplies the resource properties; omitted properties can reset to defaults, so declare all required non-default values.

questions.prompt: A company wants one identity directory for three Azure subscriptions. Which relationship is supported?

options.text: Each subscription must have a unique tenant.
options.explanation: Azure does not require a different tenant for every subscription.

options.text: Each subscription must be associated with three tenants simultaneously.
options.explanation: A subscription is associated with exactly one Entra tenant at a time.

options.text: The subscriptions must be replaced by resource groups inside Entra ID.
options.explanation: Resource groups are Azure resource containers, not substitutes for subscription-to-tenant associations.

options.text: One Entra tenant can be associated with all three subscriptions.
options.explanation: The same tenant can serve multiple subscriptions, while each subscription is associated with one tenant at a time.

questions.prompt: An application definition is used in two Entra tenants. Which object represents the application’s instance in each tenant?

options.text: A service principal.
options.explanation: A service principal is the tenant-specific representation of an application.

options.text: An organizational unit.
options.explanation: Entra ID does not use AD DS organizational units, and an OU would not represent an application instance.

options.text: An Azure subscription.
options.explanation: A subscription is a resource-management and billing boundary, not an application’s directory instance.

options.text: A Group Policy Object.
options.explanation: Group Policy Objects manage AD DS settings; they do not represent Entra application instances.

questions.prompt: A legacy Azure workload needs domain join, LDAP and Kerberos. The team wants Microsoft to operate the domain controllers. Which service best matches?

options.text: Azure resource groups.
options.explanation: Resource groups organize Azure resources; they do not provide domain authentication services.

options.text: Microsoft Entra Domain Services.
options.explanation: The managed service provides traditional domain capabilities without the team deploying and maintaining domain controllers.

options.text: Microsoft Entra ID alone.
options.explanation: Entra ID provides cloud identity protocols, not the traditional managed-domain LDAP and Kerberos interface required here.

options.text: AD DS on self-managed Azure VMs.
options.explanation: This can provide the protocols, but the team would operate those domain controllers itself.

questions.prompt: An administrator plans to organize Entra users into traditional organizational units and apply AD DS Group Policy to those units. What should they recognize?

options.text: An Entra ID P2 license adds traditional AD DS OUs.
options.explanation: Premium identity capabilities do not turn Entra ID into an AD DS OU and Group Policy directory.

options.text: Running an AD DS VM automatically converts the Entra tenant into AD DS.
options.explanation: An AD DS domain controller on a VM is a separate directory deployment, not a conversion of Entra ID.

options.text: Entra ID does not provide the traditional OU and Group Policy hierarchy.
options.explanation: Entra users and groups have a flat directory structure; traditional AD DS OU-based Group Policy is not an Entra ID feature.

options.text: Entra ID creates an OU automatically for every resource group.
options.explanation: Azure resource groups do not become Entra organizational units.

questions.prompt: A team needs policies responding to user or sign-in risk through Entra ID Protection. Which Entra ID edition discussed in this module adds that capability beyond P1?

options.text: Entra ID Free.
options.explanation: Free directory features do not include the P2 risk-based Identity Protection capability required here.

options.text: Entra ID P1 alone.
options.explanation: P1 provides Conditional Access, but the module identifies risk-based Identity Protection as a P2 addition.

options.text: No identity license is relevant if an Azure subscription exists.
options.explanation: Having an Azure subscription does not grant every premium Entra identity feature.

options.text: Entra ID P2.
options.explanation: P2 includes Identity Protection capabilities for risk-based user and sign-in protection.

questions.prompt: An App Service app should require authenticated accounts from the company’s Entra tenant. Which approach matches the module?

options.text: Configure App Service Entra authentication with the company tenant and require authentication.
options.explanation: App Service authentication can enforce sign-in using the configured tenant; requiring authentication protects access to the app.

options.text: Leave anonymous access enabled and only add company branding.
options.explanation: Branding changes appearance; it does not require an authenticated account from the tenant.

options.text: Create a new Entra tenant for every visitor.
options.explanation: A per-visitor tenant is not needed; the stated requirement is to use the company’s existing directory.

options.text: Deploy an AD DS controller solely to enable web-based Entra sign-in.
options.explanation: App Service can integrate directly with Entra authentication without deploying an AD DS domain controller.

questions.prompt: A security group should automatically include users whose Department attribute is "Finance", then remove them when that attribute changes. Which membership type fits?

options.text: Dynamic user membership.
options.explanation: Dynamic user rules evaluate user attributes and update membership when the matching attributes change.

options.text: Assigned membership maintained manually.
options.explanation: Assigned membership relies on manual additions and removals rather than attribute-based automatic updates.

options.text: Dynamic device membership.
options.explanation: Dynamic device rules select devices, not users by their Department attribute.

options.text: A list of individual direct resource permissions without a group.
options.explanation: Direct permissions do not create the required automatically maintained user group.

questions.prompt: A security group uses a dynamic device rule. What does Microsoft’s current licensing guidance require for the devices that become its members?

options.text: An Intune for Education license assigned to every device.
options.explanation: Device-based dynamic membership does not require licenses for the member devices.

options.text: No member license is required for those devices.
options.explanation: Microsoft states that devices in device-based dynamic membership groups do not require member licenses.

options.text: One Entra ID P1 user license for each device.
options.explanation: The unique-user licensing requirement for dynamic user groups does not impose a license on each device member.

options.text: One Entra ID P2 license for each device.
options.explanation: P2 is not a mandatory per-device membership license for this dynamic security group.

questions.prompt: Company Windows devices must stay joined to on-premises AD DS for machine authentication and Group Policy while also having an Entra device identity. Which state fits?

options.text: Microsoft Entra registered with only a local device account.
options.explanation: Registration for personal-device access does not provide the required existing AD DS domain join.

options.text: Workgroup devices without an Entra identity.
options.explanation: This state provides neither the requested on-premises domain join nor the Entra device identity.

options.text: Microsoft Entra hybrid joined.
options.explanation: Hybrid joined devices retain the on-premises domain join and also have an Entra device identity.

options.text: Microsoft Entra joined only.
options.explanation: Entra-only join does not retain the on-premises AD DS domain join required in this scenario.

questions.prompt: A test user was deleted from Entra ID ten days ago and has not been permanently deleted. How should you recover that account?

options.text: Create a new account and assume it is the same directory object.
options.explanation: A new account is a different object; the existing deleted account can still be restored.

options.text: Wait until day 31 for automatic restoration.
options.explanation: After the retention window, permanent deletion begins rather than automatic restoration.

options.text: Permanently delete it first, then select Restore.
options.explanation: Permanent deletion cannot be undone and would remove the available restore path.

options.text: Restore it from Deleted users.
options.explanation: The account remains restorable within the 30-day retention window unless it was permanently deleted.

questions.prompt: Users currently have direct product licenses. You want to migrate them to equivalent group-based licenses without losing services. Which sequence is appropriate?

options.text: Assign group licenses, verify successful equivalent licensing, then gradually remove direct assignments.
options.explanation: Verifying the inherited licenses before removing direct ones avoids a gap in service access; the same product is consumed only once per user.

options.text: Remove every direct assignment before assigning group licenses.
options.explanation: This can leave users temporarily unlicensed and disrupt their services or data.

options.text: Delete the user accounts, then recreate them in the licensing group.
options.explanation: Licensing migration does not require deleting identities and would unnecessarily disrupt access.

options.text: Leave direct assignments forever and assume group departure revokes all licenses.
options.explanation: Leaving a group removes inherited licensing, but retained direct assignments continue to license that user.

questions.prompt: A SaaS application exposes a SCIM endpoint. You want user creation and removal to follow the identity lifecycle automatically. Which integration fits?

options.text: Use a deployment output to return the application’s account list.
options.explanation: An ARM output returns deployment values; it does not provide ongoing SCIM provisioning and deprovisioning.

options.text: Connect the Entra provisioning service to the application’s SCIM endpoint.
options.explanation: SCIM and the provisioning service automate user and group lifecycle changes through the target application’s endpoint.

options.text: Use an Azure RBAC Reader assignment as the provisioning connection.
options.explanation: Azure RBAC controls access to Azure resources; assigning Reader does not implement SCIM account provisioning in the SaaS app.

options.text: Require administrators to create and remove every app account manually.
options.explanation: Manual account management does not meet the requirement for automated lifecycle provisioning.

questions.prompt: A workload should survive a datacenter failure while remaining in one Azure region. Which physical boundaries should you use for redundancy where supported?

options.text: Different resource names within one datacenter only.
options.explanation: Changing names provides no physical isolation from a datacenter failure.

options.text: Separate availability zones within that region.
options.explanation: Zones are physically separate datacenter groups with independent power, cooling and networking within a region.

options.text: Separate resource groups in the same availability zone.
options.explanation: Resource groups are logical management containers and do not provide separate datacenter failure boundaries.

options.text: Separate subscriptions with all VMs pinned to the same zone.
options.explanation: Subscription boundaries do not separate those VMs from the same physical zone failure.

questions.prompt: You want a supported service to replicate across availability zones automatically rather than pinning one resource to a single zone. Which deployment category should you choose?

options.text: A second resource group without changing service configuration.
options.explanation: A resource-group boundary is not a service redundancy configuration.

options.text: A second billing subscription alone.
options.explanation: A billing boundary does not enable automatic zone replication for the service.

options.text: Zone-redundant.
options.explanation: A zone-redundant service spreads or replicates across zones through the platform, unlike a single-zone placement.

options.text: Zonal, pinned to one selected zone.
options.explanation: A zonal resource is placed in the selected zone and does not by itself provide cross-zone redundancy.

questions.prompt: A temporary lab’s VMs, network and storage share the same deletion date. What organization makes cleaning up that lab straightforward?

options.text: Mix the lab resources with production resources and delete that group.
options.explanation: Group deletion affects its contained resources, so mixing production with disposable lab resources creates an unsuitable shared lifecycle.

options.text: Put every resource in several resource groups simultaneously.
options.explanation: A resource-group-scoped resource belongs to one resource group at a time, not several.

options.text: Nest a lab resource group inside a production resource group.
options.explanation: Azure resource groups cannot be nested.

options.text: Place the lab’s resources in a dedicated resource group and delete the group when finished.
options.explanation: A shared resource-group lifecycle allows the contained lab resources to be deleted together when the lab ends.

questions.prompt: A company wants development and production to have separate billing and access-management boundaries. Which structure is appropriate?

options.text: Use separate Azure subscriptions for the environments.
options.explanation: Subscriptions provide billing and access-control boundaries and can separate lifecycle environments.

options.text: Use only different VM names inside one shared resource group.
options.explanation: Resource names alone do not create separate subscription billing or access boundaries.

options.text: Use different availability zones as billing boundaries.
options.explanation: Zones provide physical resilience within regions, not independent subscription billing boundaries.

options.text: Use one tag and assume it creates a new subscription.
options.explanation: A tag can help organize cost reporting, but it does not create a separate subscription boundary.

questions.prompt: Several subscriptions need the same inherited governance policy. Where should you organize them for a shared policy assignment?

options.text: Under a storage account.
options.explanation: A storage account is a resource, not a parent container for subscriptions and policy inheritance.

options.text: Under a management group.
options.explanation: Management groups sit above subscriptions and allow governance assignments to apply across the subscriptions beneath them.

options.text: Inside one resource group spanning the subscriptions.
options.explanation: A resource group belongs to one subscription; it cannot contain other subscriptions.

options.text: Inside a single availability zone.
options.explanation: Availability zones are physical deployment boundaries, not governance containers for subscriptions.

questions.prompt: A deployment uses a region that has a paired region. The owner has not configured cross-region recovery for the service. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Availability zones are the paired region.
options.explanation: Zones are within one region; a paired region is a different regional boundary.

options.text: Creating a second resource group automatically replicates the data.
options.explanation: Resource groups organize resources but do not configure service data replication.

options.text: Check the service’s replication and recovery requirements; pairing alone does not ensure automatic failover.
options.explanation: The module explicitly warns that services may require customer-configured recovery and replication across regions.

options.text: Every resource automatically fails over because the region is paired.
options.explanation: A region pair does not give every resource automatic cross-region replication and failover.

questions.prompt: A governance team wants to assign several tagging and location policies together and track one shared compliance goal. Which Azure Policy resource fits?

options.text: A policy exemption for every resource.
options.explanation: Exemptions record exceptions to policies rather than bundling policies for enforcement and compliance tracking.

options.text: A remediation task without policy definitions.
options.explanation: A remediation task acts on applicable policy assignments; it is not a container for defining the policy set.

options.text: An initiative definition.
options.explanation: An initiative groups policy definitions so they can be assigned and tracked together for a shared goal.

options.text: One Azure RBAC role definition.
options.explanation: An RBAC role lists access permissions; it does not group configuration-compliance policy definitions.

questions.prompt: A team wants noncompliant resource requests recorded but allowed to proceed while it studies the impact. Which policy effect fits?

options.text: deny
options.explanation: deny blocks the noncompliant request, contrary to the requirement to allow it.

options.text: disabled
options.explanation: disabled prevents policy evaluation, so it does not provide the requested audit of noncompliance.

options.text: modify
options.explanation: modify changes supported request properties; the requirement is to observe rather than change them.

options.text: audit
options.explanation: audit records a warning for noncompliance without blocking the request.

questions.prompt: A deny policy allowing only Region A is assigned after a VM already exists in Region B. What does the policy do to that existing VM during a compliance scan?

options.text: Flags it as noncompliant without deleting it.
options.explanation: A deny policy evaluates existing resources for compliance but does not delete them merely because they violate the newly assigned rule.

options.text: Deletes it automatically.
options.explanation: deny blocks relevant noncompliant requests; it is not an automatic resource-deletion remediation.

options.text: Moves it automatically to Region A.
options.explanation: A deny effect does not migrate existing resources to another region.

options.text: Marks it compliant permanently because it predates the policy.
options.explanation: Resources already present are evaluated by compliance scans; creation before assignment does not automatically make them compliant.

questions.prompt: A deployIfNotExists remediation task must deploy a missing related resource. What authorization does the assignment need?

options.text: A stored human administrator password inside the policy rule.
options.explanation: Azure Policy remediation uses a managed identity rather than requiring an embedded administrator password.

options.text: A managed identity with the required Azure RBAC permissions.
options.explanation: Policy remediation uses the assignment’s managed identity, which must be authorized for the deployment it performs.

options.text: Only an identity with Reader access, even when the task must create resources.
options.explanation: Reader can inspect resources but does not grant the required creation permissions for this deployment.

options.text: No identity or permissions because policy bypasses Azure authorization.
options.explanation: Remediation does not bypass authorization; it needs a managed identity and appropriate permissions.

questions.prompt: A new deny assignment should evaluate compliance without blocking resource requests during a pilot. Which assignment setting matches?

options.text: Keep enforcementMode at Default for the deny effect.
options.explanation: Default enforces the deny effect and can block the requests the pilot is intended to allow.

options.text: Start a remediation task and assume it disables deny enforcement.
options.explanation: Remediation tasks repair applicable resources; they do not replace the assignment’s enforcementMode setting.

options.text: Set enforcementMode to DoNotEnforce.
options.explanation: DoNotEnforce retains compliance evaluation while suppressing the policy effect during resource requests.

options.text: Set the policy effect to disabled.
options.explanation: disabled prevents evaluation, so it cannot provide the desired pilot compliance results.

questions.prompt: A resource meets a policy’s intent through a different approved control. Which policy exemption category describes that reason?

options.text: Waiver.
options.explanation: Waiver records accepted noncompliance rather than the intent being met through another control.

options.text: An initiative.
options.explanation: An initiative groups policy definitions; it is not an exemption category.

options.text: An attestation for every unrelated policy.
options.explanation: Attestations record manual-policy compliance; they are not the exemption category for this accepted alternative control.

options.text: Mitigated.
options.explanation: Mitigated records that the policy’s intent is satisfied through another method.

questions.prompt: A user needs to manage VMs only in the Lab resource group and must not grant access. Which assignment best follows the exercise and least privilege?

options.text: Owner at subscription scope.
options.explanation: Owner includes access management, and subscription scope extends well beyond the requested Lab group.

options.text: Reader at the Lab resource-group scope.
options.explanation: Reader can view resources but cannot perform the requested VM-management operations.

options.text: User Access Administrator at subscription scope.
options.explanation: This role is for access management and the scope is too broad for the VM-management requirement.

options.text: Virtual Machine Contributor at the Lab resource-group scope.
options.explanation: This role and narrow scope allow VM management in the intended group without granting access-management authority.

questions.prompt: One custom role excludes an operation through NotActions, but another assigned role allows that same operation. With no deny assignment or other restriction, how are those grants combined?

options.text: The other role can grant the operation.
options.explanation: NotActions subtracts from one role’s Actions; it is not a deny that overrides permissions granted by a different role.

options.text: The first role’s NotActions blocks the operation across every role.
options.explanation: NotActions is not a global deny; RBAC combines allowed permissions across assignments.

options.text: The newest assignment always replaces every older assignment.
options.explanation: RBAC role assignments are additive, not an automatic replacement based on creation time.

options.text: Neither role applies until their definitions are merged into one role.
options.explanation: Separate assignments already combine their allowed permissions; a merged role definition is not required.

questions.prompt: A user’s Contributor assignment is inherited from the subscription. You want to remove that specific grant for the user. Which location must you address?

options.text: Move the user between availability zones.
options.explanation: Users and RBAC grants are directory/access constructs, not physical zone placements that can revoke this grant.

options.text: The subscription scope where the assignment was made.
options.explanation: An inherited assignment originates at the parent scope; remove or change that assignment there to revoke its grant.

options.text: Delete an equivalent assignment from the resource group even though none exists there.
options.explanation: Deleting a nonexistent local assignment cannot remove the actual parent-scope grant.

options.text: Rename the resource group.
options.explanation: Resource groups cannot be renamed, and naming does not revoke inherited role assignments.

questions.prompt: You are granting an application access to one storage account. Which three elements make up the Azure RBAC role assignment?

options.text: Policy effect, policy rule and compliance percentage.
options.explanation: Those concern Azure Policy compliance rather than assigning access to a principal.

options.text: Tenant branding, sign-in logo and helpdesk URL.
options.explanation: Branding and helpdesk settings do not define an Azure resource access grant.

options.text: Security principal, role definition and scope.
options.explanation: These identify who receives access, what operations are permitted and where the access applies.

options.text: Resource name, region and SKU.
options.explanation: Those describe a resource configuration, not the who, what and where of an RBAC role assignment.

questions.prompt: An administrator needs to add an Azure role assignment at a resource-group scope. Which role discussed in the module provides access-management permissions there?

options.text: Reader.
options.explanation: Reader provides resource viewing, not role-assignment write permissions.

options.text: Contributor.
options.explanation: Contributor manages resources but does not grant access by creating Azure role assignments.

options.text: Virtual Machine Contributor.
options.explanation: VM management is distinct from managing Azure RBAC role assignments; this role does not grant that access-management authority.

options.text: User Access Administrator.
options.explanation: User Access Administrator manages user access to Azure resources, including role assignments at its authorized scope.

questions.prompt: You need to investigate who created or deleted Azure RBAC assignments last month. Which view and filter match the exercise?

options.text: Azure Activity Log filtered by timespan and role-assignment operations.
options.explanation: The Activity Log records Azure RBAC changes; the timespan and operation filters isolate the relevant events.

options.text: Only the current Role assignments tab, without historical events.
options.explanation: The current assignments show existing grants but do not provide the complete history of creation and deletion events.

options.text: Only a VM’s CPU chart.
options.explanation: VM performance metrics do not identify Azure role-assignment changes.

options.text: Only the storage account’s access keys page.
options.explanation: Access keys are storage credentials, not the Activity Log history of Azure RBAC operations.
